blocks.text: Ask a model a question and it can answer from what it already knows. But the moment you want it to send an email, book a meeting, run a piece of code, or update a row in a database, knowing is not enough, something in the world has to actually change. That something is a tool. This lesson builds up the full picture of what a tool is in MCP: what makes it different from just reading data, and the exact three pieces of information every tool description is built from.
1. What a Tool Actually Is

blocks.alt: A model decides to call a tool and the effect flows back
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738064-872939695.png

A tool is a named, callable action that an MCP server exposes to a model, something the model can invoke to make a specific thing happen. It is not a fact the model can look up, it is a button the model can press. Pressing it can send a message, write a file, charge a card, or trigger a deployment, depending entirely on what the server behind that tool actually does when called.

The model itself never runs any of this code. It only ever decides, based on the conversation, that a particular tool should be called with particular arguments. The actual work, and any side effect that comes from it, happens on the server, far away from the model's own reasoning process.

code.content:
# From the model's point of view, calling a tool looks like this
result = call_tool("send_email", {"to": "alex@example.com", "subject": "Update"})
# Somewhere on a server, an actual email now gets sent because of that call

blocks.text: 2. Tools vs Resources: Do vs Read

blocks.alt: A tool performs an action while a resource is read only
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738065-991247360.png

MCP draws a clean line between two very different kinds of server capability: resources, which let a model read data, and tools, which let a model do something. A resource is passive, asking for it never changes anything in the world, it just hands back content, a file, a database row, a web page. A tool is active, calling it is supposed to cause something, and calling it twice can easily cause it twice.

This distinction matters enormously for how a host and a model should treat each capability. Reading a resource is safe to do speculatively, to explore, to retry without a second thought. Calling a tool is not, because every call is a real action with real consequences, and a model or host that treats the two the same way will eventually resend an email, place a duplicate order, or overwrite something it should not have.

blocks.title: A useful test
blocks.content: If calling a capability twice in a row, with the same arguments, produces the same observable state as calling it once, it is behaving like a resource. If calling it twice does something meaningfully different, or duplicates an effect, it is a tool, no matter what it is named.

blocks.text: 3. The Anatomy of a Tool Description

blocks.alt: A name, a description, and an input schema together form a tool description
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738065-996655567.png

Every tool a server exposes is described by exactly three pieces of information: a name, a description, and an inputSchema. Together these three fields are the entire contract between the server and anything calling it, there is nothing else a model gets to see about a tool before deciding to use it.

It helps to think of these three fields as answering three separate questions a model implicitly asks about every tool: what is this called, what does it do, and exactly what arguments does it need. Get any one of them wrong or vague, and the model's ability to use the tool correctly suffers, even if the underlying server code is flawless.
4. The Name Field

The name is the identifier the model uses to refer to the tool in every call it makes, and it is also usually the first and strongest signal the model has about what the tool does, since models are trained on enormous amounts of code and text where names carry real meaning. A tool named search_flights tells the model far more, at a glance, than one named tool_7 or process.

Good tool names are short, specific, and verb-first, describing the action rather than the general subject area. send_email is a better name than email_tool, and create_calendar_event is better than calendar, because the verb makes the effect of calling it obvious without needing to read further.

code.content:
# Weak, vague names a model has to guess about
"tool_1", "process", "handle", "doStuff"

# Strong, verb-first names that describe the action
"send_email", "create_calendar_event", "search_flights", "cancel_subscription"

blocks.text: 5. The Description Field

The description is free text explaining what the tool does, when to use it, and anything a caller needs to know that is not obvious from the name alone. This is the field that carries the most nuance, and it is the field most often under-written in practice, servers frequently ship a one-line description when the tool actually has important caveats, side effects, or preconditions worth spelling out.

A weak description says "Sends an email." A strong description says "Sends an email immediately and irreversibly to the given address. Use only after the user has explicitly confirmed the recipient and content, this action cannot be undone." The second version gives the model exactly the judgment it needs to use the tool responsibly, the first gives it nothing beyond the obvious.
6. The inputSchema Field

The inputSchema is a JSON Schema object describing exactly what arguments the tool accepts: which fields exist, what type each one is, which are required, and often a human-readable description per field. This is the piece that turns a vague natural-language intention, like "email Alex about the delay," into a precisely shaped, machine-checkable call.

Later lessons in this module go much deeper into inputSchema on its own, since it deserves a full treatment, but the short version here is that without it, a model would be guessing blindly at argument names and types, and a server would have no reliable way to validate what came in before running it.
7. Why the Model Needs All Three at Once

These three fields are not redundant, they cover different failure modes if missing. Drop the name and the model has nothing to call. Drop the description and the model may call the right tool at the wrong moment, or misunderstand a subtlety like irreversibility. Drop the inputSchema and even a model that correctly wants to call the right tool at the right time has no reliable way to build a valid set of arguments.

items: Name: tells the model what to call and hints at what the action is
Description: tells the model when and why to call it, and any caveats
inputSchema: tells the model exactly how to shape the arguments for a valid call

blocks.text: A useful exercise is to imagine each field silently deleted, one at a time, from the create_task example shown earlier. Delete the name, and the model has no token to put in a tool call at all.
Delete the description, and the model might reasonably call create_task for something that is really a calendar event instead of a to-do.
Delete the inputSchema, and the model might send title as text when the server actually expects task_title, a mismatch that only shows up as a runtime failure.
8. Side Effects: What Actually Makes a Tool a Tool

blocks.alt: A tool call changes something in the world beyond just returning data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738065-354355615.png

The defining property of a tool is that calling it changes something outside of the conversation itself. That change might be visible immediately, like a chat message being posted, or it might be invisible to the user in the moment but very real, like a background job being queued, a row being written to a database, or an external system being billed.

It is worth being honest about the fact that not every "tool" in the wild is perfectly action-shaped, some servers expose things labeled as tools that really just compute or fetch something without side effects. MCP does not forbid this, but the cleanest, most predictable servers reserve the tool category for things that genuinely do something, and use resources for things that merely read.

One way to sanity-check a candidate tool is to ask what would need to be true for calling it twice, back to back with identical arguments, to be perfectly fine. If the honest answer is "nothing bad happens," the action is mild. If the answer involves duplicate charges, duplicate messages, or duplicate records, that is a strong signal this tool needs to be called deliberately, not experimentally.
9. Idempotent vs Non-Idempotent Tools

blocks.alt: An idempotent tool is compared against a non idempotent tool
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738272-738971603.png

Among tools that do have side effects, there is an important further distinction: some are idempotent, meaning calling them again with the same arguments leaves the world in the same state as calling them once, and some are not, meaning a second identical call causes a second, separate effect.

Setting a thermostat to 70 degrees is idempotent, calling it five times in a row still leaves the thermostat at 70. Sending an email is not, calling it five times sends five emails. This distinction matters hugely for how safely a host can retry a failed call: retrying an idempotent tool after a timeout is usually harmless, retrying a non-idempotent one blindly can cause real duplicate effects.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Tool","Idempotent","Why"],"rows":[["set_thermostat_temperature","Yes","Same target value produces the same end state no matter how many times it is called"],["send_email","No","Every call sends a distinct message"],["create_ticket","No","Every call creates a new ticket, even with identical arguments"],["update_user_profile_field","Often yes","Setting a field to the same value repeatedly leaves it unchanged"]]}

blocks.text: A server can help here by explicitly noting idempotency in a tool description, since MCP itself has no dedicated field for it. A description that says "safe to call multiple times with the same input" or "each call creates a new, separate record" gives a host or model exactly the information it needs to decide how to handle a timeout or a retry.
10. Tools Are Declared Up Front, Not Guessed

blocks.alt: A server declares its tools up front rather than the model guessing
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738274-608096181.png

A model never invents a tool call out of nothing. It can only call tools that the server has explicitly declared exist, with their name, description, and inputSchema all supplied ahead of time through a discovery step. This is what keeps the whole system predictable, a model cannot decide, on a whim, to call some capability the server never advertised.

This module has an entire later lesson dedicated to exactly how that discovery step works. For now, the important point is simply that the set of tools available in any given conversation is a known, finite, server-declared list, never an open-ended guess.

This also means a tool that stops being declared effectively stops existing for that session, even if the model remembers discussing it earlier in the conversation. If a server removes a tool, or a host disconnects from that server, any later attempt to call it should fail cleanly rather than quietly succeeding against stale memory.
11. Who Decides a Tool Exists

The server author decides what tools to expose, and that decision is a real design choice, not an automatic reflection of everything the underlying system can technically do. A server wrapping a calendar system might expose create_event and list_events, while deliberately leaving out delete_all_events, even though the underlying calendar API supports it, because the server author judged that action too dangerous to hand to a model.

blocks.title: Tools are a curated surface
blocks.content: Exposing a tool is an explicit act of trust. A well-designed server exposes the smallest set of actions that gets the job done, not the largest set the underlying system happens to allow.

blocks.text: This curation decision is also where a server draws its own security boundary. A server for a codebase might expose run_tests and create_branch as tools, while deliberately leaving out force_push_to_main, not because the underlying git installation could not do it, but because the server author judged that particular action too risky to place behind a model's discretion.

items: Start from the smallest set of actions that satisfies the intended use case
Add a new tool only when a real, recurring need shows up, not speculatively
Treat every additional tool as additional exposure, not a free improvement

blocks.text: 12. Where Tools Sit in the Bigger MCP Picture

Tools do not exist in isolation, they are one of three capability categories a server can expose, alongside resources and prompts. A single server frequently offers all three at once: resources to give the model context to reason over, tools to let it act on conclusions it reaches, and prompts to offer ready-made ways of framing a request.

A useful way to picture a typical session is that resources feed the model information, the model reasons over that information, and tools are how the model then acts on whatever it decided. Tools are usually the last step in that chain, not the first.

This layering also explains why a server author should resist the temptation to fold everything into tools out of convenience. A capability that is purely informational and cheap to expose as a resource, like "read the current user's profile," is usually better modeled as a resource, keeping the tool list focused on things that genuinely act.
13. Read-Only Tools: A Blurry Edge Case

blocks.alt: A read only tool sits in a blurry edge case between tool and resource
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738275-184058194.png

Not every tool cleanly fits the do versus read split. Some servers expose a tool like search_flights, which does not change any state anywhere, it just performs a computation or an external lookup too complex or too parameterized to fit the resource model. MCP allows this, and many real-world servers use tools this way.

The way to think about this edge case is that the resource versus tool line is really about shape, not strictly about side effects. Resources are addressed by a fixed or templated URI and read directly. Tools are invoked with arbitrary structured arguments and can express far richer, parameterized behavior, even when that behavior happens to be read-only underneath.

A practical rule of thumb: if a capability needs rich, varied input to produce its result, like a flight search taking an origin, destination, date range, and cabin class, it usually belongs as a tool, even without side effects, because the resource model of a fixed or lightly templated URI does not comfortably express that much variation.
14. Naming and Describing Tools for a Model Audience

Because the only consumer of a tool description is a model deciding whether and how to call it, every field should be written with that reader in mind, not a human skimming API documentation. Ambiguity that a human developer might resolve by reading source code is invisible and unresolvable to a model, which only ever sees the description text.

items: Prefer specific verbs over vague nouns: send_email, not email_action
State irreversible or costly effects explicitly in the description
Mention any precondition the caller must satisfy, like needing a valid user id first
Avoid internal jargon or abbreviations that only make sense to the team that built the server

blocks.text: It is worth testing a tool description the same way you would test documentation meant for a new hire who has never seen the codebase: read only the name, description, and schema, nothing else, and ask whether a reasonable person could construct a correct call from that alone. If the answer is no, the description needs more work, not the model.

Requires a valid ticket_id; does nothing to tickets that do not exist."],["Sends a message.","Posts a message to a specific Slack channel immediately and visibly to all channel members; cannot be recalled once sent."]]}

blocks.text: 15. A Minimal End-to-End Tool Example
Putting all three fields together end to end, here is a complete, realistic tool description for a small task-management server, followed by what a model actually sends when it decides to use it.

code.content:
# What the model sends when the user says "remind me to call the bank tomorrow"
call_tool("create_task", {"title": "Call the bank", "due_date": "2026-07-08"})

blocks.text: Notice that the due_date field is absent from the required list in that schema. The model is still free to include it, and a well-designed server should handle its absence gracefully, defaulting to no due date rather than rejecting the call outright. Optional fields like this let a single tool cover both a quick, bare-minimum call and a fuller, more specific one.

code.content:
# A caller can also omit the optional field entirely
call_tool("create_task", {"title": "Buy milk"})

blocks.text: Worked Example

Consider a customer support server exposing two capabilities: a resource for reading a customer's order history, and a tool for issuing a refund. The model is asked, "This customer says their package never arrived, can you help?"

A well-built host feeds the model the order history resource first, letting it read what actually happened. Only after reasoning over that information does the model decide to call issue_refund, with the specific order id and amount as arguments, an action with a very real financial side effect that should never be triggered blind, before the read step.

code.content:
# Step 1: read, no side effect
history = read_resource("orders://customer/8841/history")

# Step 2: reason, then act, real side effect
result = call_tool("issue_refund", {"order_id": "ORD-2291", "amount": 42.50})

blocks.text: Notice the shape of that sequence: read first to gather grounding, act second, deliberately, with specific arguments tied to what was just read. That ordering, read before act, is a pattern worth recognizing across almost every well-designed MCP-powered workflow.
Common Mistakes

items: Exposing a tool that is really just a read, and naming it like an action, which misleads a model about whether it is safe to call more than once.
Writing a one-line description that omits an important side effect, like irreversibility or a real-world cost, leaving the model to call it without understanding the consequences.
Treating idempotent and non-idempotent tools the same way when deciding whether to retry a failed or timed-out call.
Assuming the model can infer argument names or types that are not actually present in the inputSchema.
Exposing the broadest possible action an underlying system allows, like delete_all, instead of the narrower action an assistant actually needs.
Giving two different tools confusingly similar names, which increases the odds a model calls the wrong one.

blocks.title: A quick smell test
blocks.content: If you cannot answer, in one sentence, what real-world thing changes when this tool is called, that is a sign it may actually be a resource wearing a tool's name, worth revisiting before shipping it.

blocks.text: Practice

Take a system you know well, a note-taking app, a project tracker, anything with real state. Write out a tool description, with name, description, and a rough inputSchema, for exactly one action in that system. Then answer, in a sentence each: is this tool idempotent, and what is the worst-case consequence if a host retries this call automatically after a timeout without checking.

As a stretch, sketch a second tool for the same system that would be a bad idea to expose to a model at all, something too broad or too destructive, and write one sentence explaining what narrower tool you would expose instead to cover the same underlying need more safely.
Key Takeaway

A tool is a named action a server exposes, described completely by three fields, a name, a description, and an inputSchema, and calling it is meant to cause a real effect rather than just return information. That single distinction, do versus read, is the reason MCP treats tools and resources as separate concepts with different safety assumptions.

The next lesson in this module zooms all the way into that third field, inputSchema, and works through JSON Schema in real depth: the types it supports, how required and optional fields are expressed, and exactly how a model turns a schema into a valid, structured call.
